passage: I'm Thomas, and I'm ten. On Sports Day, my best friend Chinmay won the drawing competition. His picture of rain on our school roof got first prize. When they called his name, I clapped so hard my hands went red. I shouted "Chinmay!" so loudly that the teacher looked at me. I was really, really happy for him. He had practised every lunch break. But when I saw my own drawing on the board with no ribbon, I felt a small pinch inside. I wanted a ribbon too. Both feelings were there at the same time. After school we shared his prize chocolate on the steps, and the pinch mostly went away.

qa.q: What was Chinmay's winning picture of?
qa.a: Rain on the school roof.

qa.q: What two feelings did Thomas have at the prize-giving?
qa.a: Real happiness for Chinmay, clapping till Thomas's hands went red, and a small pinch of wanting a ribbon too.

qa.q: What helped the pinch go away, and what does that show?
qa.a: Sharing the prize chocolate with Chinmay on the steps; staying close to a friend made room for both the joy and the small wish.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt hearing Thomas shout his name?
qa.a: Chinmay probably felt proud and cared for, knowing his best friend was truly happy for him 😊

grounding: A child cheers loudly for a friend's prize and feels warm joy alongside a small pang of wanting one too.

passage: Class 4 note, spelling bee day. By Sharmila, class teacher. When Rhea won the final round, the loudest clapping came from Rhea's best friend, Minakshi, who had been knocked out in round three. Minakshi jumped up, clapped above her head and hugged Rhea before Rhea had even collected the trophy. A minute later I saw her look at the trophy and then down at her shoes, just for a moment. I think a small pang was there too, and that is natural. At break I told Minakshi, "You were a wonderful friend today. And round three was hard. Want to practise some tricky words together next week?" She grinned and said yes. I'll keep two lunch breaks free.

qa.q: In which round was Minakshi knocked out?
qa.a: Round three.

qa.q: What does Minakshi looking at the trophy and then at her shoes suggest?
qa.a: Alongside real joy for Rhea, she may have felt a small pang of wishing she had won too.

qa.q: How did Sharmila respond to both of Minakshi's feelings?
qa.a: Sharmila praised her as a wonderful friend, said round three was hard, and offered practice together, so both the joy and the wish were respected.

qa.q: What was it like for Rhea to be hugged by Minakshi before collecting the trophy?
qa.a: Rhea likely felt extra happy and supported, knowing a friend who had been knocked out was celebrating so warmly.

grounding: A teacher notes a girl cheering her best friend's win with real joy while a small pang shows for a moment.

passage: Saturday. Dear diary, Kishore won the inter-school chess tournament today!!! I was there when he checkmated the boy from the other school. I jumped up and clapped so loud the arbiter said "Shh!" I didn't care. Kishore taught me chess in Class 3, so it's like half my win too. 😊 Okay, truth: when they gave him the big trophy, I felt a tiny bit jealous. I lost in round two. I wanted to be up there. But mostly I was proud. Both feelings are true, I think. Tomorrow I'm asking him to teach me the move he used. Ujjwal

qa.q: In which round did Ujjwal lose?
qa.a: Round two.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel when Kishore got the big trophy?
qa.a: Mostly proud, with a tiny bit of jealousy at wanting to be up there too.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal plan for tomorrow, and why is it a good choice?
qa.a: To ask Kishore to teach the winning move, turning the small jealousy into learning and time together.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel about Ujjwal's loud clapping?
qa.a: Kishore would likely feel happy and supported, especially as he taught Ujjwal chess back in Class 3.

grounding: A child cheers Kishore's chess win with real pride, while admitting a tiny pang of jealousy.

passage: At the Pola fair in Kinhi, the school's rangoli contest was judged under the big neem. Preeti, ten, had drawn a peacock. Her best friend Vijay had made a bullock pair in orange and green, every bell drawn with a matchstick. When the headmaster read out, "First prize, Vijay Wankhede!" Preeti jumped up and clapped so hard her bangles clinked. "Vijay! Vijay!" He went pink and grinned at her. She was glad, truly glad; he had practised on his courtyard floor for a week. Then she glanced at her peacock, with no ribbon beside it, and something small pinched inside. She wished there had been a ribbon for her too. But when Vijay ran over with his prize, she grabbed his arm and swung it high, laughing.

qa.q: What did Vijay draw for the rangoli contest?
qa.a: A bullock pair in orange and green, with every bell drawn with a matchstick.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when she glanced at her own peacock?
qa.a: A small pinch of wishing for a ribbon, sitting alongside her real gladness for Vijay.

qa.q: What could Preeti say to herself about the pinch she felt?
qa.a: That wanting a prize herself is normal and doesn't cancel her happiness for Vijay; she could practise her peacock for next year.

qa.q: How might Vijay feel with Preeti cheering loudest?
qa.a: Vijay probably feels shy but very happy, with his best friend celebrating his win so openly.

grounding: A child cheers her friend's prize with real warmth while a small wish for herself sits underneath.

passage: In the school hall in Rotterdam, the poetry prize was the last thing announced before the holidays. Elif, eleven, had written about her grandmother's garden. Her best friend Vera had written about the sea. When Mr Jansen said, "The winner is Vera Kowalczyk!" Elif was the first on her feet, clapping and whistling, which she'd only just learned to do. Vera went bright red. Elif felt warm all over; she'd heard Vera read that poem aloud on the tram and knew it was good. Then, as Vera walked up for the book token, Elif thought of her own poem, still folded in her bag, and a small ache came and sat quietly beside the warmth. On the way out, she hugged Vera anyway. "Read it to me again on the tram?"

qa.q: What did Vera's winning poem describe?
qa.a: Vera wrote about the sea.

qa.q: What shows that Elif feels real warmth for Vera, even with the small ache?
qa.a: She's first on her feet, whistling, and hugs Vera afterwards asking to hear the poem again; the ache sits beside the warmth rather than replacing it.

qa.q: What small step could Elif take with her own folded poem?
qa.a: She could share it with Vera on the tram too, or ask Mr Jansen for feedback, turning her wish into her next try.

qa.q: How might Vera feel hearing Elif's whistle first?
qa.a: Vera probably feels embarrassed but delighted, knowing her best friend is proud of her.

grounding: A child cheers her friend's win with genuine warmth while a small wish for herself sits beneath.
